--- title: Chat with your data 💬 subtitle: Build LLM-powered apps with shinychat, querychat and ggsql author: "Nelson Amaya" description: "Put a language model inside your Shiny apps: streaming chat UIs with shinychat, natural-language data filtering with querychat, and SQL that draws its own charts with ggsql." categories: - LLM - shiny - shinychat - querychat - ggsql - SQL date: "2026-07-04" date-modified: last-modified order: 2 level: Intermediate duration: 45 min track: Work with AI prerequisites: "Talking to machines" image: her.gif editor_options: chunk_output_type: console aliases: - /sessions_workshop/10-llm-apps/10-llm-apps.html citation: url: https://nelsonamayad.github.io/R4DEV/sessions_ai/02-llm-apps/02-llm-apps --- > *"The most profound technologies are those that disappear."*
--Mark Weiser In [Make it shine](/sessions_workshop/08-shiny/08-shiny.qmd) you built Shiny apps where users interact through sliders and dropdowns. In the previous session, [Talking to machines](/sessions_ai/01-llm/01-llm.qmd), you learned to call an LLM from code. This session welds the two: apps where the interface is **a conversation**, and where the model translates human questions into the filters, queries and charts you used to build by hand. Everything runs on the same [`ellmer`](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org/) chat objects from the previous session, so your API key setup carries over unchanged. ::: {.lesson-info} **Level:** Intermediate  ·  **Time:** ~45 min  ·  **Prerequisites:** Talking to machines  ·  **Tools:** shinychat, querychat, ggsql ::: ## You will learn to - Embed a streaming chat UI inside a Shiny app with shinychat. - Let a user filter data with natural language using querychat. - Write SQL that draws its own chart with ggsql. - Understand why `querychat_app()`'s convenience wrapper isn't meant for production deployment, and what to use instead. ## PART I: A chat UI in one line The [**`shinychat`**](https://posit-dev.github.io/shinychat/r/) package provides the chat interface --the streaming text, the message bubbles, the input box-- so you never build them from scratch. The quickest possible start is genuinely one line: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(shinychat) shinychat::chat_app(ellmer::chat_google_gemini()) # <1> ``` ::: 1. `chat_app()` takes any ellmer chat object and wraps it in a complete running Shiny app. Try it now --it is the fastest way to poke at a system prompt interactively. For a real app you compose the pieces yourself: `chat_ui()` in the interface, `chat_append()` in the server. Here is a complete teaching assistant --note how the system prompt does all the personality work, exactly as in the previous session: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(shiny) library(bslib) library(shinychat) ui <- bslib::page_fillable( theme = bslib::bs_theme(bootswatch = "journal"), h4("R4DEV teaching assistant 🤖"), shinychat::chat_ui("chat", fill = TRUE) # <2> ) server <- function(input, output, session) { chat <- ellmer::chat_google_gemini( # <3> system_prompt = paste( "You are the teaching assistant of R4DEV, a tidyverse-first R workshop.", "Answer questions about R with short runnable examples.", "Always use the native pipe |> and never suggest base R plotting." ) ) observeEvent(input$chat_user_input, { # <4> stream <- chat$stream_async(input$chat_user_input) # <5> shinychat::chat_append("chat", stream) # <5> }) } shinyApp(ui, server) ``` ::: 2. `chat_ui()` drops the whole chat interface into your layout, like any other Shiny widget. It fills the page like the dashboards from session 8. 3. The chat object is created **once per user session** --it carries the conversation memory, so follow-up questions work. 4. Whatever the user types arrives as `input$chat_user_input` --a plain Shiny input, nothing exotic. 5. `$stream_async()` returns the answer as it is generated, and `chat_append()` streams it into the UI word by word. Async matters: while one user waits for an answer, the app stays responsive for everyone else. Download it and run it yourself:

{{< downloadthis r4dev-chat-app.R dname = r4dev-chat-app label="Download the chat app" icon=download type=info >}} ::: callout-tip ## Where's the live demo? This minimal version is deliberately un-grounded --it answers from the model's general training, nothing more. Rather than deploy a second, redundant chat app, R4DEV ships **one** live chat demo: [**Ask R4DEV**](/sessions_ai/03-ragnar/03-ragnar.qmd#capstone-ask-r4dev) in the next session, which uses this exact `shinychat` interface but answers only from *retrieved* R4DEV content. Build this one locally first --then see why the next session grounds it. ::: ## PART II: querychat, or the end of the filter sidebar Now the genuinely new idea. In session 8's earthquakes app, filtering data meant building a sidebar of inputs --one widget per variable, wired to `filter()` calls. [**`querychat`**](https://posit-dev.github.io/querychat/r/) replaces that whole apparatus: the user *asks* for the subset they want, the LLM writes **SQL**, and your app reacts to the result. The safety design deserves attention before the code: **the model never sees your data and never executes anything.** It only reads the table's *schema* --column names and types-- and proposes a read-only `SELECT` statement, which querychat runs locally against a [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) copy of your data frame. Hallucinated SQL fails loudly; it cannot delete, modify or leak a single row. We'll point it at an old friend --the Spotify archive from session 2: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(querychat) songs <- readr::read_csv("spotify_favorites_archive.csv") querychat::querychat_app( # <6> songs, table_name = "songs", client = ellmer::chat_google_gemini(), # <7> greeting = "Ask me anything about these 1,178 songs — in plain language.", data_description = paste( # <8> "One row per song from the discographies of 8 artists,", "with Spotify audio features saved before the API closed in 2024.", "valence and energy run from 0 to 1.", "cover_url holds the album cover image address." ) ) ``` ::: 6. Like `chat_app()`, `querychat_app()` is the batteries-included version: data table, chat sidebar, live SQL display. It is built for your own machine: under the hood it launches a Shiny *gadget* that picks its own port, which a hosting platform can't find, so the deployed app fails its start-up health check. For custom layouts, and for anything you deploy, use the modular pieces instead: `QueryChat$new()` plus `qc$sidebar()` and `qc$server()` inside an ordinary `shinyApp()`. 7. Any ellmer chat works. Translating questions to SQL is easy work --a small, cheap model does it fine. 8. The `data_description` is your prompt-craft moment: tell the model what a row *means* and what units the columns use. Good descriptions are the difference between "it just works" and confused SQL. Once it runs, try these --and **watch the SQL it writes** (querychat shows it; always read it, that's your audit trail): - *"Only songs by Oasis, most energetic first"* - *"Songs sadder than 0.2 valence but with energy above 0.8"* --angry music, in other words - *"Which artist has the happiest average discography?"* Get the app:

{{< downloadthis r4dev-querychat-app.R dname = r4dev-querychat-app label="Download the querychat app" icon=download type=info >}} Or try it live below --this deployed instance is built from those modular pieces and runs on **Claude Sonnet 5** via `ellmer::chat_anthropic()`, with the API key set as a server-side environment variable on Posit Connect Cloud (never in the code, never exposed on this page). Everything else --the SQL-writing, the safety model, the UI-- is exactly what you just read. :::: column-screen-inset :::: ## PART III: SQL that draws: ggsql You just watched an LLM write SQL for you --which makes this the right moment to meet [**`ggsql`**](https://r.ggsql.org/), a brand-new tool from Posit (alpha, April 2026) that extends SQL with a `VISUALISE` clause borrowed straight from the grammar of graphics you learned in session 2. One language selects the data *and* draws it. These chunks run **live in this page** through ggsql's knitr engine --the `r:` prefix lets SQL read data frames straight from the R session: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggsql) library(tidyverse) songs <- readr::read_csv(paste0(getwd(), "/spotify_favorites_archive.csv")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.ggsql .sql .cell-code} SELECT artist, AVG(valence) AS mean_valence FROM r:songs GROUP BY artist VISUALISE mean_valence AS x, artist AS y DRAW bar ``` ```{=html} ``` ::: Aggregation in SQL, mapping and geometry in the `VISUALISE` clause: `mean_valence AS x` is exactly `aes(x = mean_valence)` wearing a SQL costume. One more, with color as a third channel: ::: {.cell} ```{.ggsql .sql .cell-code} SELECT valence, energy, artist FROM r:songs VISUALISE valence AS x, energy AS y, artist AS color DRAW point ``` ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: callout-warning ## Alpha software `ggsql` is an **alpha release** --the syntax may still change, and you will hit rough edges. That is not a reason to avoid it; it is a reason to pin the version in your projects and read the [release notes](https://r.ggsql.org/) when you update. Watching a tool this young is also watching how the R ecosystem evolves in real time. ::: Why does ggsql belong in this session? Because of what you saw in Part II: **LLMs are remarkably good at writing SQL.** A model that can answer *"show me energy against valence, coloured by artist"* with a complete ggsql query --data selection and chart in one statement-- is a very short step from the querychat app you just ran. The pieces on this page are the ingredients of the next generation of data tools; now you know how each one works alone. ::: callout-tip ## Next: teach the model to answer *only* from real sources Everything here answers from what the model already knows. The next session, [**Grounded in truth**](/sessions_ai/03-ragnar/03-ragnar.qmd), builds the other half: retrieval-augmented generation with **`ragnar`** --a chatbot that answers questions about R4DEV itself, grounded only in the workshop's actual content, including a live capstone app. ::: ## 🏗 Practice 2: Ship it {.unnumbered} Every exercise here talks to a live model or runs an app, so you'll need your own R session and an API key (the Gemini free tier works). ::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"} # Basic - Change the chat app's system prompt so it refuses to answer anything not related to R, politely - Run the querychat app and find the five *angriest* songs (low valence, high energy). Read the SQL it generated --would you have written it differently? ::: ::: {.callout-important icon="false" collapse="true"} # Intermediate - Point `querychat_app()` at the Maddison GDP data from session 2 and ask it three questions you answered with dplyr back then. Compare the SQL to your pipes - Rewrite the ggsql scatter above to show only songs with valence below 0.5, faceted by artist --check the [ggsql docs](https://r.ggsql.org/) for the FACET syntax ::: ::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"} # Advanced - Combine this lesson with [Talking to machines](/sessions_ai/01-llm/01-llm.qmd): build a Shiny app with a `chat_ui()` where the model has a *tool* that runs `ggsql_execute()` on the songs table and returns the chart. You will have built a tiny data analyst ::: ## Key takeaways - shinychat, querychat and ggsql all wrap the same idea: let the model translate a human question into code that already works. - A convenience wrapper built for interactive/local use (like `querychat_app()`) is not automatically safe to deploy -- check what it actually runs underneath. - Natural-language filtering is only as good as the SQL it generates -- always be able to read what the model wrote. - Everything here answers from the model's general knowledge; the next lesson changes that. ::: {.continue-learning} [← Previous: Talking to machines](/sessions_ai/01-llm/01-llm.qmd) [Track overview: Work with AI →](/learn/ai.qmd) [Next: Grounded in truth →](/sessions_ai/03-ragnar/03-ragnar.qmd) :::
